subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: Preparing for the Mela — Students discuss how they prepare themselves for a trip (p. 21)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the story of Nita, Radha, and Dadiji getting ready for the mela — packing water bottles, waiting for Mohan Chacha's family, and persuading Dadiji to come along. Students listen and picture the scene.

Class discussion opens with the prompt on Textbook p. 21: 'How do you prepare yourself for a trip?' Students share what they pack, who they coordinate with, and how older family members are included in their own outings. Teacher notes responses on the board under two columns: 'Things we carry' and 'People we plan with'.

Teacher guides a second layer of discussion: how the story shows neighbours and extended family acting as one group. Students compare this with their own community or neighbourhood practices — who helps organise, who looks after elderly or younger members, what makes an outing feel safe and welcoming for everyone.

Students write two or three sentences in their notebooks about one person in their family or neighbourhood who needs special help during outings and how they can support that person. Pairs share their sentences aloud if willing.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how a community group plans and organises a shared outing, including making it accessible for members who need support.
periods.section_context: Nita, Radha, Dadiji preparing for mela outing; packing water bottles; coordinating with neighbours Sneha and Rohit; waiting for Mohan Chacha's family arriving by train; persuading mobility-limited Dadiji to join; extended family and neighbours as a single social unit.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What would happen if nobody helped Dadiji — would she still come?' This surfaces the value of inclusion without naming it as a concept. Invite students who live in joint or extended families to share how their outings are planned.

periods.section_ref: On the Way to the Mela
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Way to the Mela — Students discuss what transport they take to travel within their city, town, or village (p. 24)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of the group at the bus stop and inside the bus (p. 24)

time_bands.activity: Teacher narrates the journey: the group walks carefully to the bus stop, boards bus number 401, the conductor helps Dadiji to a reserved seat, Rohit's father buys tickets for everyone, and children are told not to lean out. Students follow along in Textbook p. 24 and identify who does what during the journey.

Class discusses the two prompts on Textbook p. 24: first, students describe briefly any trip they have taken with friends, neighbours, or family; second, they share what transport they use to travel within their own city, town, or village. Teacher lists the modes named by the class on the board — walking, bus, train, autorickshaw, cycle, etc.

Teacher draws attention to the safety behaviours shown in the story — walking carefully, not leaning out of windows, the reserved seat for an older passenger — and asks students to recall similar rules they follow or have seen adults follow. Discussion connects the story's road etiquette to students' lived experience of travelling.
Students write in their notebooks: the name of one transport mode they commonly use and two safety rules that apply to it. Teacher invites two or three students to share what they have written.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify different modes of transport used in a community and describe safety behaviours associated with each.
periods.section_context: Walking to the bus stop; bus number 401; conductor helping Dadiji to reserved seat for older people; Rohit's father buying tickets; rule about not leaning out of window; modes of transport — bus, train, autorickshaw.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think there is a special seat for older people on the bus — is it a rule or is it kindness, or both?' This invites students to think about designed civic structures versus voluntary caring behaviour. Where students mention local modes not in the textbook (tempos, ferries, tongas), affirm and add them to the board list.

periods.activity_title: What Happens at the Mela — Safety and Service
periods.textbook_anchor: At the Mela — Students write the purpose of the Lost and Found booth (p. 29)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of the mela entrance showing the map, Lost and Found booth, Help Booth, First Aid, ambulance, police jeep, and fire engine (p. 29)

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes the group arriving at the mela's parade ground — pointing to Textbook p. 29 illustration — and names each facility shown at the entrance: map of stall locations, Lost and Found booth, Help Booth, First Aid, ambulance, police jeep, fire engine. Students look at the illustration and identify each feature as it is named.

Students answer the two Write tasks from Textbook p. 29 in their notebooks: what is the purpose of the Lost and Found booth, and what is the role of the police dog. Teacher circulates, prompting students to think about what problem each facility solves — who needs it and when.

Class shares answers. Teacher guides discussion on why a large community gathering like the mela needs emergency vehicles and help services — connecting to students' own experience of crowded places (markets, fairs, temple visits). The Find out prompt from p. 29 — why fire engines and ambulances are present — is discussed orally as a whole class.

Students make a quick two-column table in their notebooks: 'Facility at the Mela' and 'Who it helps / What problem it solves', filling in at least four rows from what was discussed. Teacher checks a few notebooks for completeness.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify community safety and service facilities in a public space and explain the role each plays in keeping people safe.
periods.section_context: Mela at parade ground; map at entrance showing stall locations; Lost and Found booth; Help Booth; First Aid; ambulance; police jeep; fire engine; police dog.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you got separated from your family at a crowded place, which booth would you go to first, and why?' This makes the safety infrastructure personally meaningful rather than abstract. Encourage students to recall if they have seen similar facilities at local fairs or markets.

periods.textbook_anchor: At the Mela — Students study the sketch and answer questions about location and route (p. 30)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook neighbourhood sketch showing parade ground, Nita's house, Sneha and Rohit's house, police station, school, bank, post office, library (p. 30)

time_bands.activity: Teacher orients students to the neighbourhood sketch on Textbook p. 30 — pointing out what the map shows: houses, the parade ground, the police station, and other landmarks. Students identify north, south, east, and west if marked, and name the landmarks they can spot.

Students work individually through the four questions in the activity on Textbook p. 30: circling Sneha and Rohit's house, circling Nita and Radha's house, deciding whose house is closer to the parade ground, and tracing the route from the police station to the parade ground naming the places passed. Teacher moves around the room prompting students who are uncertain about how to read directions or estimate distances on the sketch.

Class shares answers. Teacher draws the route from police station to parade ground on the board, inviting students to call out the landmarks in order. Discussion focuses on how to describe a route clearly — using 'turn left', 'pass the bank', 'next to the school' — connecting map-reading to language.

Students write a two-sentence description in their notebooks of the route from police station to parade ground, using at least two landmark names from the sketch. This bridges map-reading to verbal route description.

periods.implied_lo: Students can read a simple line drawing of a neighbourhood to locate landmarks and describe a route between two points.
periods.section_context: Neighbourhood sketch on p. 30; parade ground; Nita and Radha's house; Sneha and Rohit's house; police station; school; bank; post office; library; route from police station to parade ground.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you could only use landmarks — no left or right — how would you tell a friend how to get from the police station to the parade ground?' This pushes students toward landmark-based wayfinding, which is how many communities navigate. Pair students who find the sketch difficult with a peer who can point rather than explain verbally.

periods.activity_title: Sketching My Route from Home to School
periods.textbook_anchor: At the Mela — Students sketch the route from home to school that they follow every day (p. 31)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook neighbourhood sketch (p. 30) retained as a reference model

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the neighbourhood sketch on Textbook p. 30 — now used as a model — and draws attention to how houses, roads, and landmarks are shown as simple shapes and lines with labels. Students note that a sketch does not need to be perfectly to scale; it needs to be readable.

Students draw their own route from home to school in the space provided on Textbook p. 31, marking at least three landmarks they pass (a shop, a tree, a temple, a crossing, a pond — whatever is real for them). They label each landmark. Teacher circulates, asking individual students to narrate their route as they draw.

Students pair up and explain their sketch to each other as if giving directions to someone who does not know the way. Partners ask one clarifying question each. Teacher listens to a few pairs and highlights examples of clear landmark use or inventive symbols.
Quick whole-class share: two or three students hold up their sketches and name one landmark they included. Teacher affirms the variety of routes and landmarks across the class.

periods.implied_lo: Students can draw a simple sketch map of a familiar route, marking landmarks and using labels to make it readable to another person.
periods.section_context: Route from home to school; personal landmarks (shops, trees, crossings, temples, ponds, etc.); sketch with labels; Textbook p. 31 drawing space.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What would happen if your map had no labels — could your partner still follow it?' This draws attention to the function of labels and symbols. Accept any landmarks meaningful to each student's local context; regional diversity in landmarks is expected and valuable.

periods.activity_title: Mela Roles and the Matching Activity
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students pick a suitable word from the list, match it with a picture, and write the word below the picture (p. 32)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pictures of mela roles: firefighter, halwai, toy seller, puppeteer, bangle seller, volunteer, police officer, medical attendant, mehendi artist (p. 32)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the three discussion prompts on Textbook p. 32: how can we care for our elders, what kinds of vehicles do we see around us, and how can we ensure safety during travel. Students respond briefly to each in a whole-class conversation, with teacher capturing key phrases on the board.

Students complete the matching activity on Textbook p. 32 individually — picking the correct word from the list (firefighter, halwai, toy seller, puppeteer, bangle seller, volunteer, police officer, medical attendant, mehendi artist) and writing it below the matching picture. Teacher prompts students who are unsure about less familiar roles by asking what the person in the picture is doing or carrying.

Class checks answers together. For each role, teacher invites a student to say one sentence about what that person does at the mela and why their role matters. Discussion broadens to include whether students have seen these roles at fairs or markets in their own area — connecting the textbook mela to students' lived experience of community gatherings.
Students choose one mela role from the list and write a sentence in their notebooks: 'The [role] at the mela helps by ___.' Teacher reads a few aloud to close the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify the roles of different community helpers in a public gathering and explain the contribution each makes.
periods.section_context: Matching activity p. 32; mela roles: firefighter, halwai, toy seller, puppeteer, bangle seller, volunteer, police officer, medical attendant, mehendi artist; discussion prompts on caring for elders, types of vehicles, travel safety.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you know someone who does one of these jobs — at a fair or in your neighbourhood?' This connects textbook roles to local community members students may recognise. Where students know regional names for these roles (e.g. halwai may be known by a different term locally), affirm and note those alongside the textbook word.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students organise a mock mela in the classroom using locally available materials (p. 33)
materials: Locally available materials: toys, puppets, play money, miniatures, clay models, small objects from school

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the mock mela task from Textbook p. 33 aloud and facilitates a quick planning discussion: what stalls will the class set up, what roles are needed, and who will take which role. Groups of four or five are formed, each assigned a stall type (food, toys, services such as help booth or first aid, entertainment). Each group spends the opening phase deciding their stall name and what they will display or do.

Groups set up their stalls using whatever locally available materials are to hand — toys, clay shapes, drawings of items, play money made from paper, or small classroom objects standing in for goods. Teacher circulates, prompting groups to think about how to welcome visitors, keep their space clean, and stay in role. Students who are buyers move between stalls, interact with sellers, and use play money for transactions.

A brief whole-class debrief: teacher asks each group to name their stall and one thing they noticed during the mock mela — something that worked well, something that was tricky, or a rule they found themselves following (queueing, paying, keeping the area tidy). Teacher draws connections between what students did and the mela behaviours read about in the chapter.
Students draw and label one vehicle they see near their school or home in their notebooks, completing the Draw task from Textbook p. 33 as a quiet close to the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can plan and enact the roles and functions of a community gathering, making decisions about organisation, fairness, and shared responsibility.
periods.section_context: Mock mela in classroom; roles planned and enacted — stalls, buyers, sellers; locally available materials: toys, puppets, play money, miniatures, clay models; drawing and labelling vehicles near school and home (p. 33).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask during the debrief: 'Did anyone in your group need help during the mela — what did you do?' This surfaces inclusion and peer support as naturally enacted values. Encourage groups to name their stalls in local languages or use local names for foods and crafts.

assessment_items.question_text: Nita's family wanted Dadiji to come to the mela even though it was far and she found it hard to walk. What does this tell us about how they planned their outing?

options.label: A
options.text: They made sure everyone in the group, including Dadiji, was included and supported.

options.label: B
options.text: They left Dadiji at home because long trips are not suitable for elderly people.

options.label: C
options.text: Dadiji was the one who organised the whole outing for the family.

options.label: D
options.text: They planned the outing only for the children and neighbours, not for family elders.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item checks whether students grasped that inclusive planning — persuading and supporting Dadiji — was central to the preparation, not incidental.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how a community group plans and organises a shared outing, including making it accessible for members who need support.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student holds the misconception that elderly people should be excluded from outings rather than supported — misses the inclusion theme of the section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the role of the person being supported (Dadiji) with the person doing the organising — a role-attribution error within the same section.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student incorrectly recalls the group as children-and-neighbours only, forgetting that family elders were both participants and recipients of care in the planning.

assessment_items.question_text: The group used three different modes of transport to reach the mela. Name two of these modes and give one safety rule that applies to each.
expected_elements: Names at least two modes from: walking, bus, train, autorickshaw.
Gives a safety rule for the first mode named (e.g. walking — look both ways, stay on the footpath; bus — do not lean out of windows, stay seated).
Gives a safety rule for the second mode named (e.g. train — wait for the train to stop before boarding; autorickshaw — hold on and stay seated).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per correctly named mode (up to 2) and one mark per plausible safety rule linked to that mode (up to 2). A total of 4 marks is possible. Accept any reasonable safety rule consistent with the mode named; region-specific transport modes (tempo, ferry, tonga, cycle rickshaw) are acceptable if the student uses them and provides a matching safety rule.
assessment_items.chapter_section: On the Way to the Mela
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify different modes of transport used in a community and describe safety behaviours associated with each.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Names at least two modes from: walking, bus, train, autorickshaw.
Gives a safety rule for the first mode named (e.g. walking — look both ways, stay on the footpath; bus — do not lean out of windows, stay seated).
Gives a safety rule for the second mode named (e.g. train — wait for the train to stop before boarding; autorickshaw — hold on and stay seated).

assessment_items.question_text: At the mela's entrance there was a Lost and Found booth. A child who loses her bag at the mela should go there because —

options.label: A
options.text: it is the place where lost items are kept and people can find things that belong to them.

options.label: B
options.text: it is the booth that sells the cheapest items at the mela.

options.label: C
options.text: it is where children can buy tickets for rides and games.

options.label: D
options.text: it is the place where the police keep items confiscated from stall owners.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item checks direct comprehension of the Lost and Found booth's function as described in the section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify community safety and service facilities in a public space and explain the role each plays in keeping people safe.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses the Lost and Found booth with a commercial stall — has not grasped the service (non-commercial) role of the facility.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the Lost and Found booth with a ticketing or entertainment counter — conflates support services with recreational facilities at the same venue.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student invents a punitive or enforcement function for the booth not present in the section — draws incorrectly on a partial understanding of the police presence at the mela.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the neighbourhood sketch from the chapter. Whose house is closer to the parade ground — Nita and Radha's or Sneha and Rohit's? If you walk from the police station to the parade ground, name two places you would pass through.
expected_elements: Correctly identifies which house is closer to the parade ground based on the sketch.
Names one place passed when walking from the police station to the parade ground.
Names a second place passed on that route.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark for correctly identifying the closer house (answer depends on the textbook sketch — accept the answer consistent with p. 30). Award one mark each for up to two correctly named intermediate landmarks on the police-station-to-parade-ground route as shown in the sketch. The specific landmarks are fixed by the textbook sketch; accept any landmark that genuinely lies on the path as drawn.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a simple line drawing of a neighbourhood to locate landmarks and describe a route between two points.

competency.competency_text: Explains a line drawing of their school, village, and ward

expected_elements: Correctly identifies which house is closer to the parade ground based on the sketch.
Names one place passed when walking from the police station to the parade ground.
Names a second place passed on that route.

assessment_items.task: Draw a sketch of the route from your home to school. Mark at least three landmarks you pass on the way and write a label next to each one.
assessment_items.scaffold: Start by drawing your home at one corner of the page. Then draw the roads you walk along. Add the three landmarks you pass — they could be a shop, a tree, a temple, a crossing, a well, or anything else you see every day. Write the name of each landmark next to it. Finally, draw your school at the other end.
format_of_output: A hand-drawn sketch on the notebook page
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the sketch shows a recognisable path from home to school with at least three landmarks that are labelled. The landmarks will vary by student and region — accept any real landmark the student encounters on their route. Neatness is not assessed; legibility of labels and presence of a clear route line are the key markers.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can draw a simple sketch map of a familiar route, marking landmarks and using labels to make it readable to another person.

competency.competency_text: Draws a sketch of their school, village, and ward using symbols and directions

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can translate a lived, familiar route into a spatial representation with labelled landmarks — the core skill of simple sketch-map making.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold walks students through a start-point, path, landmarks, labels, and end-point sequence. Students who follow all five steps will produce a complete sketch. Those who draw the route but omit labels need a prompt: 'Can you write the name of what you drew?'
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a clear directional path, three or more legibly labelled landmarks, both home and school marked. Weak: a collection of disconnected drawings with no path connecting them, or a path with no labels.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who have difficulty drawing may dictate their route to the teacher or a peer, who writes the landmark names while the student draws the shapes. Students who walk a very short route may use objects inside the school compound as landmarks.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook task and the chapter's map-reading strand both require students to produce a personal spatial representation — a sketch is the natural output and allows regional and individual variation in landmarks.

assessment_items.question_text: At the mela, one of the people working there makes and sells sweets. Another repairs and demonstrates puppets. Which row correctly matches these two workers to their roles?

options.label: A
options.text: Sweet maker and seller — halwai; puppet maker and demonstrator — puppeteer.

options.label: B
options.text: Sweet maker and seller — volunteer; puppet maker and demonstrator — mehendi artist.

options.label: C
options.text: Sweet maker and seller — toy seller; puppet maker and demonstrator — bangle seller.

options.label: D
options.text: Sweet maker and seller — medical attendant; puppet maker and demonstrator — firefighter.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item tests whether students can match two specific community roles — halwai and puppeteer — to their functions, drawn directly from the matching activity in the section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the roles of different community helpers in a public gathering and explain the contribution each makes.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has not distinguished occupational roles from civic-support roles — confuses halwai (a food trade role) with volunteer and puppeteer with mehendi artist, suggesting the role labels were not meaningfully connected to their functions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student substitutes nearby commercial roles (toy seller, bangle seller) for the correct ones — indicates partial recall where 'seller' was retained but the specific product/craft was confused.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student maps both roles to emergency service workers — confuses the category of community helper entirely, conflating food and craft roles with safety-service roles present in the same chapter.

assessment_items.task: With your group, plan a small mock mela for your classroom. Decide: (a) what stalls you will have, (b) who will run each stall, and (c) one rule your mela will follow to keep everyone safe and happy. Write your plan, then act it out.
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1 — List two or three stalls your group will set up (for example: a toy stall, a food stall, a help booth). Step 2 — Write one name next to each stall to show who is in charge. Step 3 — Write one shared rule for the whole mela (for example: put rubbish in the bin, be kind to all visitors, help anyone who looks lost). Step 4 — Use what is in your classroom to set up and run your stalls for a short time.
format_of_output: A written group plan listing stalls, roles, and one shared rule
A brief enactment with students in their assigned roles
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the written plan and the enactment together. Look for: at least two stalls named, a named role-holder for each, and one explicit shared rule. During enactment, observe whether students stay in role and apply the rule they wrote. Groups that name their stalls in local languages or use regional foods and crafts should be affirmed — regional variation is expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can plan and enact the roles and functions of a community gathering, making decisions about organisation, fairness, and shared responsibility.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether students can collaboratively investigate the organisation of a community event, allocate roles deliberately, agree on a shared norm, and enact the plan — the full inquiry-and-action cycle at a Grade III level.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The four-step scaffold separates planning from doing. Groups that skip directly to enactment without a written plan should be guided back to Step 1 — the written plan is the inquiry record. Step 3 (shared rule) is where values and dispositions become explicit; teacher should listen for rules that connect to chapter themes (safety, cleanliness, helping others).
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a written plan with named stalls and role-holders, a rule that connects to the chapter's civic themes (not just 'be quiet'), and an enactment where students interact in role. Weak: a list of stalls with no role assignment, or an enactment that abandons the planned rule immediately.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Groups may use any available materials — drawings of goods count as stall displays if physical objects are not available. Students who find writing difficult may dictate their part of the plan to a group member.
